Summary:
Quick kickoff to align on POC success criteria, workload sizing, benchmarks and an initial quality evaluation plan (golden prompts, regression tests, hallucination checks, scoring). AE + SE from Redwood (Maya, Liam) with Edgecase Retail ML + Platform + Product. Actionables: share benchmark sheet, upload logs, draft golden prompts and rubric.

Topics covered:
- What counts as success for the pilot (business & ML metrics)
- Target traffic and latency/throughput sizing (peak vs p50/p95)
- Benchmark plan: load, accuracy, hallucination, format checks, failover behavior
- Quality eval specifics: golden prompts, paraphrase families, regression test cadence, scoring approach (automated + human), acceptance gates
- Timeline and next steps

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on this account, and with me is Liam Ortiz, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Nina Patel: Hey Maya, doing good. Thanks.
[00:08] Carlos Ruiz: Morning all, Carlos here.
[00:10] Sophie Lane: Hi, Sophie. Excited to get going.
[00:13] Maya Chen: Great. Quick agenda — confirm pilot goals, review workload numbers, discuss quality eval plan — golden prompts and regression, and then next steps. Does that work?
[00:21] Nina Patel: Yep, sounds good. We're trying to be pragmatic — our product team wants an initial pilot within four weeks. Key thing is we need reliable hallucination controls and consistent formatting for downstream ingestion.
[00:32] Liam Ortiz: Cool, understood. When you say formatting — is that strict JSON schema output, or a looser structured text?
[00:38] Sophie Lane: Mostly strict JSON. We have downstream pipelines that need fields like product_id, price, and normalized_description. If the model spits out funky arrays or omits fields, it breaks the ETL.
[00:48] Maya Chen: Okay that helps. For success criteria, we typically split into two tracks: operational SLOs (latency, p95 < 400ms for interactive flows, throughput for batch) and quality SLOs (hallucination rate, schema compliance, user-acceptance). Wanted to capture Edgecase's thresholds — what are you comfortable with?
[01:07] Nina Patel: For hallucination, our product team wants under 1% for the golden cases and under 5% on random production-like traffic. For schema compliance we want > 99% field presence on critical keys.
[01:19] Carlos Ruiz: And on latency, we can tolerate p50 of 120-150ms, p95 under 450ms. Our control plane is in us-west-2. We'll run the pilot against Redwood Dedicated or Private — still deciding.
[01:31] Liam Ortiz: Noted. For Dedicated we've seen those p95 numbers at similar sequence lengths, but it depends on tokenization and average prompt length. Can you share typical prompt sizes?
[01:39] Nina Patel: Typical user prompt is 120 to 300 tokens, but with retrieval augmented context it can spike to 2k tokens. 80% of requests are small, 20% big.
[01:49] Maya Chen: Perfect — that distribution is exactly what we need for workload sizing. For the bench plan I propose: 1) baseline functional correctness tests (golden prompts), 2) regression suite (randomized paraphrases), 3) hallucination stress tests (adversarial prompts + long context), 4) load tests (peak concurrency + steady-state), and 5) format/schema validation checks.
[02:11] Sophie Lane: Can you expand on golden prompts? How many, and what's the paraphrase strategy?
[02:16] Liam Ortiz: Sure — golden prompts are a curated set of canonical inputs we'd expect to pass with high fidelity. We'll create families: a core canonical prompt plus 4-6 paraphrases per family to ensure robustness. Golden set size typically 80-120 families for this scope; each family has 5 variants -> ~400-600 test items. Human labels will mark the expected fields and acceptable variations.
[02:38] Nina Patel: 400 tests sounds ok. We can provide 50 high-priority cases and you can expand. Important: include negative cases for hallucination detection — when the model should say "unknown" or return empty, we don't want made-up values.
[02:51] Maya Chen: Good point. We'll include explicit negative golden cases where the correct behavior is "no result". Our hallucination checks will measure 1) extraneous facts in required fields, and 2) inventing entities. We'll tag each golden case with expected hallucination status.
[03:06] Carlos Ruiz: On regression cadence, how often will we run the full set? Every check-in or nightly? We need to understand compute and cost.
[03:14] Liam Ortiz: For initial pilot, recommend nightly automated runs of the reduced regression (smoke) suite, and full regression weekly. The reduced suite would be 10-15% of the full golden set focused on critical flows. Cost depends on model/quantization, but we'll estimate in the benchmark spreadsheet.
[03:29] Sophie Lane: What about scoring? We need a simple pass/fail per case but also aggregate metrics.
[03:35] Maya Chen: We'll propose a scoring approach combining automated checks and human review. Automated scoring: schema pass/fail, token-level string metrics (BLEU / token overlap), and field-level exact match or normalized fuzzy match. We'll compute per-case scores and then aggregate to an overall quality score (weighted): 50% automated accuracy, 30% human acceptability on sampled items, 20% hallucination penalty. Passing threshold can be set to 85 overall with no more than 1% hallucinations on golden set.
[04:04] Nina Patel: 85 seems reasonable as a starting point. We may adjust weights, but that gives us a clear gate.
[04:09] Liam Ortiz: For human review, typical workflow is a small adjudication panel — you can label 50-100 items per week during pilot to calibrate. We'll provide a labeling UI export.
[04:19] Maya Chen: Let's also talk about format checks. We'll run schema validators on every output and keep a detailed error taxonomy: missing_field, malformed_json, wrong_type, extra_entities, and semantic_mismatch. That taxonomy feeds regression prioritization.
[04:33] Carlos Ruiz: Good. On the infra side, our VPC prevents 0.0.0.0/0 egress unless approved. We'll need to know data paths for Private deploy. Also curious about key management — we use AWS KMS with custom CMKs.
[04:46] Maya Chen: For Private we'll integrate with your KMS via customer-managed keys; we'll include the security pack. For hosted/Dedicated we also support KMS and HSM integrations. I'll share the SOC2 summary and the private deployment checklist after this call.
[04:59] Sophie Lane: Can Redwood run the initial load tests against a sandbox first? We want to validate load without affecting prod.
[05:03] Liam Ortiz: Yes, sandbox load test is standard. We can also do a small canonical stress test where we synthetic-augment your traffic to hit the 95th and 99th percentile sizes. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 latency and CPU/GPU utilization.
[05:17] Nina Patel: For benchmarking we need the following outputs: latency percentiles, tokens/sec, cost per 1k tokens, schema pass rate, hallucination rate, and human acceptability score.
[05:27] Maya Chen: We'll include those metrics in the benchmark sheet. We'll also run model variant comparisons — e.g., open model small quant vs larger float model and show tradeoffs in latency/quality/cost.
[05:37] Carlos Ruiz: Competitors brought up? We evaluated Anthropic and an in-house self-hosted approach. Core concern for us is predictable cost and ability to run private.
[05:47] Maya Chen: Understood. Redwood's dedicated and private modes are designed for that — but we'll quantify cost and perf tradeoffs.
[05:54] Sophie Lane: On timelines — we said product wants a pilot in four weeks. Is that feasible?
[05:59] Liam Ortiz: Yes, if we get logs and the golden seed cases within the next five business days, we can have an initial golden set and an automated regression baseline in ~2 weeks, and run load tests in week 3, then hand over pilot report week 4. That matches your ask but it's tight.
[06:16] Nina Patel: We'll aim to provide logs and 50 seed cases by 2026-05-20. Hope that's doable.
[06:22] Maya Chen: Great. We'll send a kickoff email after this with the benchmark sheet link, the golden prompt template, and the security pack.
[06:29] Carlos Ruiz: A few nitty-gritty questions — when you run hallucination detection, do you use entity linking to a knowledge base, or heuristics?
[06:36] Liam Ortiz: We use a mix: automated heuristics (out-of-vocab names, improbable dates) and an optional entity-check against a customer-provided canonical dataset. For this pilot, if you can give us the product catalog snapshot, we can enable catalog linking to flag invented SKUs.
[06:49] Sophie Lane: We'll provide a CSV of product ids and canonical names.
[06:52] Nina Patel: Also want to capture edge cases — long context + retrieval mistakes. Please include adversarial prompts that attempt to confuse the model.
[06:59] Liam Ortiz: Absolutely, we'll include an adversarial subset and log failure modes.
[07:03] Maya Chen: Any blockers on your side right now?
[07:05] Nina Patel: Only the logs export and confirming whether we can use Dedicated or Private. We'll get internal approval on Private if needed.
[07:12] Maya Chen: OK. Recap of next steps: Maya to share security + benchmark sheet, Liam to push golden prompt template and initial rubric, Nina and Carlos to share logs and product catalog, schedule pilot kickoff week of 2026-05-25.
[07:25] Sophie Lane: Thanks — that was useful.
[07:28] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email.
